PMGT1852 Week 09

PMGT1852 Week 09 - Starting a Facilitated Session: Inform, Excite, Empower, Involve (IEEI)

Overview

How a facilitated meeting is opened shapes everything that follows. This week covers:

• The IEEI framework - Inform, Excite, Empower, Involve - and the four questions participants want answered in the first 15 minutes.

• The recommended eight-step opening sequence, in which introductions come seventh rather than first.

• Excite: the most important and hardest step of the opening.

• Involve: getting participants to state their personal objectives immediately, and winning their buy-in to the agenda.

• Ground rules for how the group will work together, including ELMO, the XYZ tactic and "always look up".

• Parking boards for issues, decisions and actions.

• Effective introductions using the "gifts and hook" format.

Key Concepts

The secret to opening

The opening must first address the participants' own most important concerns. Before anything else on the agenda, people need to know what is in the meeting for them and what part they play in it.

IEEI in the first 15 minutes

Before the agenda is discussed, participants want the answers to four questions:

Why are we having this session?

What do we need to have accomplished when we are done?

What is our role in the decision making?

Why should I invest the time?

The four IEEI steps answer these questions.

The four IEEI steps

• Inform - review the purpose of the meeting and the products (deliverables) it should produce.

• Excite - paint a clear vision of the overall result and of the benefits to the participants themselves. This is the most important and the hardest step.

• Empower - explain the important role they play, why each of them was selected, or the authority given to them.

• Involve - as early as possible, draw out their personal objectives, the issues that must be covered, the challenges to overcome, or other topics that contribute to the overall goal.

Empower is not Involve. Empower tells participants that their contribution matters; Involve actually lets them contribute, by having them speak and shape the session from the start.

Starting questions (Type A and Type B)

To involve participants, the facilitator asks a starting question - the question that opens discussion of an agenda item.

• A weak, Type A question is abstract or overly technical, focuses on what the facilitator wants to know, is hard for participants to picture, and tends to produce silence. Example: "What are the inputs to the timetable process?"

• A strong, Type B question uses the participants' own language, addresses them directly, is action-oriented and open-ended, and creates a concrete situation they can see themselves in. Example: "Think about the last time you hired someone - the hurdles you had to jump over. What problems were there with the process?"

Ground rules

Ground rules are group norms that the participants agree on. They set the expected level of behaviour for the interaction, state explicitly what is acceptable and what is not, and, once agreed, become self-governing: participants enforce them on each other without the facilitator having to intervene.

Parking boards

Parking boards are prepared charts where participants' comments, suggestions, issues and resolutions are captured when they do not belong to the current agenda item. They are prepared before the meeting, and they let the group set a topic aside without losing it.

Frameworks and Formulas

The eight-step opening sequence

Welcome.

Session purpose and products (Inform, Excite, Empower).

Participants' objectives (Involve).

Agenda.

Ground rules.

Parking boards.

Introductions.

End of the opening and on to the first major agenda item.

Introductions are step 7, not step 1: by the time people introduce themselves they already know why they are here and what they will accomplish.

Involving participants (immediately after IEE)

Ask participants for their objectives for the session, or the topics most important to them.

Why:

• It involves them immediately.

• It shows that their needs are being taken into account.

• It gives an opportunity to adjust the agenda.

Tip: split the room into groups of 3-7 people, each with a team leader. Each group identifies personal objectives or issues; the leader writes them on a large visible sheet (such as A3 paper). Set a time limit. Then cluster the sheets by topic area and connect the personal objectives to the agenda items.

Gaining buy-in to the agenda

After the opening statement and the collection of personal objectives, walk through the agenda: explain the steps the group will take and the deliverable or product of each step, so participants can link their own objectives to the plan.

How to link objectives to the agenda:

Review the personal objectives one at a time, ideally grouped by category.

For each one, ask which agenda item covers it.

Circle the objectives that no agenda item covers.

Return to the circled items and decide with the group whether to leave them for a later session or to change the agenda.

Why it works: participants understand what each agenda item is for, they see where their own concerns are covered, and their buy-in to the agenda increases.

Ground rules the facilitator can propose

The facilitator proposes a first set of ground rules, invites participants to add more, and briefly explains the meaning and use of each. A standard set:

Ground rule

What it means

Everyone speaks

Say it in the room rather than afterwards; use hand signals to ask the group to speed up or slow down

One conversation

Only one conversation at a time

Take a stand

Choose an option; say what would work, not only "that won't work"

Question first

Replace a negative with a question: "Help me understand - how would that work?"; respect keeps ideas flowing

ELMO

"Enough, Let's Move On!" - triggers an immediate group vote; the majority decides, so no single person can end a discussion alone

eManners

Phones on silent; no messages or email during the session

Recharge

A group-created activity of at most 15 seconds combining a movement and a phrase, called on when energy drops (for example around 1:30 pm)

Your role / my role

Participants contribute actively and help use the time productively; the facilitator provides clarity of purpose and deliverables, a process, and an environment where everyone can be heard

Start and end on time

Take about a 10-minute break every 90 minutes, and restart on time

Use the parking boards

Issues, Decisions, Actions

Applying a ground rule: "always look up" and the XYZ tactic

When a participant reacts negatively to every suggestion ("That won't work!"), the desired behaviour is: for any suggestion, first say what you like about it and how to make it better, instead of spending time explaining why something cannot work.

The XYZ tactic introduces this as a ground rule, in three parts:

• X - state the problem behaviour: "We could identify all the reasons why this won't work."

• Y - state the consequence or the reason for change: "That would waste our time."

• Z - state the desired behaviour: "Always look up - tell us what you like and how to make it better."

Parking boards in practice

Why use them: they keep the meeting on track, let participants correct themselves, ensure off-topic items are still discussed eventually, and show that every comment is taken seriously.

Typical boards:

• Issues list - topics to be discussed later, in or after this meeting.

• Decisions list - the group's decisions, kept for the record.

• Actions list - three columns: Action, Who, When.

• Optionally: potential strategies, additional research needs.

Effective introductions: gifts and hook

A team that will work together for a year and does not know each other may need half a day of team building; a half-day meeting needs about 10-15 minutes. Use an introduction format that serves the meeting purpose, for example a name plus what the person can bring to the team's success. Have people write first, then speak.

Gifts and hook: each person names the three gifts they bring to the team's success, and the one hook - what must happen to keep them engaged and coming back.

Procedure: in the preparation stage, decide the purpose, the time and the process; write the question on a flip chart; give participants about 1 minute to write; set a per-person time limit (for example 30 seconds, using an alarm).

Worked Examples

Excite: two versions of the same opening

Both versions share the same Inform sentence: over the next two days the group will develop a plan to improve the hiring process.

• Version 1 (organizational benefit): "This matters because the organization can then hire the right people quickly."

• Version 2 (the participants' own pain): "Employees without the skills or the attitude you need make your work harder. This is your chance to get the people you need."

Version 2 is the stronger, more personally relevant statement: it speaks to the participants' own experience rather than to an abstract organizational benefit, which is exactly what Excite is meant to do.

A full opening for the hiring-process case

• Inform: Thank the participants for coming. State the problem with the hiring process - slow timeliness, wrong hires, rapid turnover - and the products of the session: a new process design plus an implementation plan.

• Excite: Use the participants' own pain, as in Version 2 above.

• Empower: "Each of you was personally selected by the leadership team. They believe you have the knowledge and the vision, and they look forward to your recommendations."

First impressions last: plan in advance exactly what you will say in the opening, so your attention goes to the participants rather than to finding the words.

Applying IEEI to a workshop

Suppose a workshop aims to improve data-transfer speeds for regional students. The four steps translate directly into an opening script:

• Inform: State the goal of the workshop and the products it will produce.

• Excite: Connect faster transfer speeds to the participants' own concerns.

• Empower: Explain how their knowledge will shape the solution being designed.

• Involve: Ask each person to name one concern they want the workshop to address.
